title: The Transformer Architecture
summary: Self-attention, multi-head attention, positional encoding, the residual+LayerNorm block, why this shape won.
html:
Many widely used language models use a decoder-only transformer. The architecture has been remarkably stable since 2017 — the changes that stuck (rotary position embeddings, pre-norm residuals, gated FFN activations, grouped-query attention) are refinements to a shape that was essentially right the first time. Understanding this block in mechanical detail is the prerequisite for everything else in this reference, because scaling laws, MoE, long-context tricks and inference optimization are all statements about this architecture.

The pre-transformer world and the sequential bottleneck

Before 2017 the default sequence model was the recurrent neural network, in practice the LSTM (Hochreiter & Schmidhuber, 1997) or the GRU. An RNN processes a sequence one position at a time, carrying a fixed-size hidden state forward:

h_t = f(W_h @ h_{t-1} + W_x @ x_t)

The fatal property is the data dependency in that recurrence. Computing h_t requires h_{t-1}, which requires h_{t-2}, and so on. This is not merely an inference-time cost — it is a training-time cost, and that distinction is what killed RNNs at scale. Even though the entire target sequence is known in advance during training, the model still cannot evaluate position 500 until it has evaluated positions 1 through 499. Training time therefore scales with sequence length no matter how many GPUs are available, because the parallelism a GPU offers cannot be applied along the sequence axis. You can parallelize across the batch, but not across time.

The second problem is path length between distant positions. For information at position 1 to influence the prediction at position 500, it must survive 499 sequential multiplications by the recurrent weight matrix. Gradients flowing back along that path shrink or explode geometrically — the vanishing/exploding gradient problem. The LSTM's gating mechanism was designed precisely to create a more additive path for gradient flow, and it genuinely helped, but it mitigated rather than removed the issue. The effective context of a well-trained LSTM was on the order of hundreds of tokens, not hundreds of thousands.

Attention already existed as a fix, bolted onto RNNs. Bahdanau et al. (2014) introduced attention for neural machine translation so that a decoder could look back at all encoder states rather than squeezing the source sentence through one fixed-size vector. The insight of Vaswani et al. (2017), in Attention Is All You Need, was that the recurrence was the part worth deleting: if attention gives every position direct access to every other position, the recurrence is doing no essential work. Removing it makes the path length between any two positions O(1) and makes the whole sequence computable in parallel during training. That parallelism — not any representational superiority in the abstract — is the reason the transformer scaled and the RNN did not.

Scaled dot-product attention

Attention is a differentiable, content-addressed lookup. Each position emits a query (what am I looking for), a key (what I can be matched on) and a value (what I hand over if matched). The three are linear projections of the same input:

Q = X @ W_Q     # (n, d_k)
K = X @ W_K     # (n, d_k)
V = X @ W_V     # (n, d_v)

attention_output = softmax(Q @ K.T / sqrt(d_k)) @ V

Read the formula from the inside out. Q @ K.T is an n × n matrix of dot products: entry (i, j) measures how well position i's query matches position j's key. The softmax over each row turns those raw scores into a probability distribution summing to 1, so row i becomes a set of mixing weights over all positions. Multiplying by V produces, for each position, a weighted average of every position's value vector. The output at position i is thus a content-selected summary of the whole sequence, with the selection learned rather than fixed by position.

The sqrt(d_k) denominator is not cosmetic, and the paper's footnote explaining it is worth internalizing. Suppose the components of q and k are independent with mean 0 and variance 1. Their dot product q · k = sum over i of q_i k_i is a sum of d_k independent zero-mean terms, so it has mean 0 and variance d_k — standard deviation sqrt(d_k). As the head dimension grows, the logits fed to the softmax therefore spread out proportionally to sqrt(d_k). With d_k = 128, typical logits are already on the order of ±11, and softmax over logits that far apart is nearly one-hot.

Why saturation is fatal rather than merely undesirable. The gradient of a softmax that has collapsed onto one entry is approximately zero everywhere — the derivative p_i(δ_ij - p_j) vanishes when p is near one-hot. A saturated attention head therefore receives almost no gradient signal and stops learning. Dividing by sqrt(d_k) renormalizes the logit variance back to roughly 1 regardless of head dimension, which keeps the softmax in its responsive regime and keeps gradients alive. This is the same class of reasoning behind careful weight initialization: control the variance of what flows through each layer so the nonlinearity operates where it has a useful derivative.

Multi-head attention

Rather than one attention operation over the full model dimension d_model, transformers run h attention operations in parallel over dimension d_head = d_model / h, then concatenate and project:

head_i   = softmax(Q_i @ K_i.T / sqrt(d_head)) @ V_i
MultiHead = concat(head_1, ..., head_h) @ W_O

The parameter and FLOP count is deliberately held roughly constant. Because d_head = d_model / h, splitting into more heads does not add parameters — it partitions the same projection matrices. Multi-head attention is therefore not a capacity increase; it is a structural constraint on how that capacity is used, and it is close to free.

The reason to prefer many small heads over one large one is that softmax averaging is destructive. A single attention head produces one distribution over positions and one weighted average. It must commit to a single notion of relevance per position. But a token frequently needs several unrelated things simultaneously: the syntactic subject it agrees with, the antecedent of a pronoun, the matching open-bracket, the topic of the paragraph. One head must blend these into a single averaged distribution, and averaging distinct signals loses them. Several heads let the model attend to different relational patterns concurrently and keep them in separate subspaces until W_O recombines them.

Interpretability work has confirmed this is what actually happens. Analyses of trained models have identified heads with legible, specific jobs — notably induction heads, which implement the pattern “find the previous occurrence of the current token and copy what followed it,” described by Olsson et al. (2022) in In-context Learning and Induction Heads and argued there to be a major mechanism behind in-context learning. Others include previous-token heads and duplicate-token heads. The caution is that head specialization is a tendency rather than a guarantee: many heads are polysemantic, some are prunable with little loss, and clean single-function heads are the exception rather than the rule.

The head-count tradeoff has an interior optimum. More heads means finer-grained relational patterns but a smaller per-head dimension, and below roughly 64 dimensions per head the individual heads lose representational precision. Most production models land at d_head of 64 or 128 and derive the head count from d_model.

Positional encoding

Attention as defined is permutation-equivariant: it is a sum over positions with weights determined by content alone, so shuffling the input shuffles the output identically and nothing else changes. The model literally cannot distinguish “dog bites man” from “man bites dog”. Position information must be injected explicitly, and how to do it is one of the few parts of the architecture that genuinely changed after 2017.

SchemeMechanismRelative?ExtrapolationStatus
SinusoidalFixed sin/cos of varying frequency added to embeddingsNo (absolute)Defined at any length, but weak in practiceOriginal (Vaswani et al., 2017)
Learned absoluteA trainable embedding per position indexNo (absolute)None — undefined past trained lengthGPT-2 / GPT-3, BERT
ALiBiLinear distance penalty added to attention logitsYesGood; strong recency biasPress et al., 2021
RoPERotates Q and K by a position-dependent angleYes (emerges from the rotation)Good, and extensible via scalingModern default (Su et al., 2021)

The original sinusoidal scheme added a fixed vector to each input embedding, built from sines and cosines at geometrically spaced frequencies. The appeal was that the offset between two positions is expressible as a linear function of the encodings, in principle letting the model learn relative offsets, and that it is defined for positions never seen in training. In practice models did not extrapolate well with it, and much of the field moved to simply learning one embedding vector per position — simpler and slightly better in-distribution, but with no meaning at all beyond the trained context length.

Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE), from RoFormer (Su et al., 2021), is the modern standard and is used by the Llama family, Mistral, Qwen and most current open-weight models. Instead of adding anything to the embeddings, RoPE takes each pair of adjacent dimensions in q and k, treats the pair as a point in a 2-D plane, and rotates it by an angle proportional to the absolute position. Different dimension pairs rotate at geometrically spaced frequencies, so low-frequency pairs encode coarse position and high-frequency pairs encode fine position.

theta_i  = 10000 ** (-2i / d)        # per-pair frequency
angle    = position * theta_i        # rotate by this
# applied to (q_2i, q_2i+1) as a 2-D rotation, likewise for k

The elegant property is that the dot product of two rotated vectors depends only on their relative offset. Rotating q by angle mθ and k by nθ makes their inner product a function of (m - n)θ, because the absolute rotations cancel in the dot product. So RoPE is applied using absolute positions but the attention scores it produces are purely relative — you get relative-position behavior with absolute-position bookkeeping, and no extra parameters. This is why it extrapolates more gracefully than a learned absolute table: an unseen position index is not an unseen embedding lookup, it is simply a rotation by a larger angle, an operation the model has a continuous handle on. The caveat is that extrapolation is graceful, not free; pushing far past the trained length still degrades quality, which is exactly what the RoPE-scaling methods in section 6 exist to repair.

The block: residuals, normalization, and pre-norm vs post-norm

A transformer layer is two sublayers — attention, then a position-wise feed-forward network — each wrapped in a residual connection and a normalization. The ordering of those two wrappers is a small-looking detail with large consequences at depth.

# Post-norm (original, Vaswani et al. 2017)
x = LayerNorm(x + Attention(x))
x = LayerNorm(x + FFN(x))

# Pre-norm (modern default)
x = x + Attention(LayerNorm(x))
x = x + FFN(LayerNorm(x))

The residual connection is the load-bearing element. Adding the input back to the sublayer output creates an uninterrupted additive path from the embeddings to the final layer — the “residual stream.” Gradients flow back along it without being multiplied by any weight matrix, which is what makes very deep stacks trainable at all. It is also the right mental model for interpretability: each sublayer reads from the residual stream, computes something, and writes its result back by addition, so the stream is a shared communication channel that all layers append to rather than a pipeline that transforms and discards.

Why pre-norm won. In post-norm the normalization sits on the residual path, so the clean additive highway is interrupted at every sublayer and gradient magnitudes get rescaled repeatedly on the way back. Deep post-norm models are correspondingly hard to start: they typically require a learning-rate warmup and are sensitive to initialization, and without care the loss diverges early in training. Pre-norm moves the normalization inside the branch, leaving the residual path a pure sum from input to output. This makes deep models markedly more stable and much less warmup-sensitive, which is why essentially all large models today are pre-norm. The tradeoff reported in the literature is that post-norm can reach slightly better final quality when it can be made to train, and that very deep pre-norm stacks see the residual stream's magnitude grow with depth — a final normalization before the output projection is standard, and some models add extra normalization to control the growth.

RMSNorm replaced LayerNorm in most recent models. LayerNorm subtracts the mean and divides by the standard deviation, then applies a learned gain and bias. RMSNorm (Zhang & Sennrich, 2019) drops the mean-centering and the bias, dividing only by the root-mean-square:

LayerNorm(x) = g * (x - mean(x)) / sqrt(var(x) + eps) + b
RMSNorm(x)   = g * x / sqrt(mean(x**2) + eps)

It is cheaper and empirically loses nothing, which is the whole justification — the re-centering term turns out not to be doing much work.

The feed-forward sublayer, where the parameters live

The FFN is applied independently and identically at every position — it is the part of the block with no cross-token interaction whatsoever. Classically it projects up by 4×, applies a nonlinearity, and projects back down:

FFN(x) = W_2 @ activation(W_1 @ x + b_1) + b_2
# W_1: (d_model, 4*d_model)   W_2: (4*d_model, d_model)

This is where most of the parameters actually are, which surprises people who think of transformers as “attention models”. Per layer, the four attention projections contribute about 4 * d_model<sup>2</sup> parameters while the two FFN matrices contribute about 8 * d_model<sup>2</sup> at the classic 4× expansion — roughly a 2:1 split in the FFN's favor. Attention is the part that moves information between positions; the FFN is the part that holds most of the model's capacity. This is directly relevant to section 4, because MoE replaces precisely this sublayer — the biggest and most parallel-friendly chunk of parameters — rather than touching attention.

The standard reading of the FFN is a key-value memory. W_1's rows act as pattern detectors over the residual stream and W_2's columns are the corresponding contributions written back, so the sublayer behaves like a large associative store: detect a pattern, add the associated information. Geva et al. (2021) argued this explicitly, finding that individual FFN units correspond to human-interpretable input patterns. Treat this as a useful and well-supported frame rather than a complete account — superposition means individual units are usually not cleanly interpretable one-to-one (see section 14).

SwiGLU is the modern replacement and appears in the Llama and PaLM families among others. Introduced by Shazeer (2020) in GLU Variants Improve Transformer, it adds a multiplicative gate: one projection produces the values, a second produces a gate, and they are multiplied elementwise.

SwiGLU_FFN(x) = W_2 @ ( swish(W_gate @ x) * (W_up @ x) )
# three matrices instead of two, so the hidden dim is
# usually shrunk from 4*d_model to ~(8/3)*d_model
# to keep the parameter count roughly matched

The gate lets the network suppress or pass information multiplicatively rather than only additively, which empirically buys a small but consistent loss improvement at matched parameter count. Note the expansion-factor adjustment: because SwiGLU uses three matrices rather than two, implementations reduce the hidden dimension to roughly 8/3 * d_model so the comparison against a 4× ReLU FFN stays parameter-fair. Missing this is a common source of confused parameter arithmetic when reading model configs.

The block, assembled

One pre-norm decoder block: each sublayer reads a normalized copy of the residual stream and adds its result back, leaving the residual path an uninterrupted sum.

The full model is this block repeated N times, preceded by a token embedding lookup and followed by a final norm and a projection to vocabulary logits (the “unembedding”, frequently weight-tied to the input embedding to save parameters). Depth and width are the two axes: GPT-3 175B used 96 layers at d_model = 12288 with 96 heads. The ratio of depth to width is itself a mild design choice, but models cluster in a fairly narrow band of aspect ratios.

Causal masking and the decoder-only design

For a language model trained to predict the next token, position i must not see positions > i — otherwise the task is trivial, the model reads the answer, and it learns nothing that transfers to generation. This is enforced by adding a mask to the attention logits before the softmax:

scores = Q @ K.T / sqrt(d_k)
scores = scores + mask          # mask[i][j] = 0 if j <= i else -inf
weights = softmax(scores)       # -inf entries become exactly 0

Using -inf rather than zeroing after the softmax is the correct implementation, because softmax normalizes over the row: masking before means the future entries contribute exactly nothing to the denominator, whereas zeroing afterwards would leave a distribution that no longer sums to 1.

The payoff of causal masking is training efficiency, and it is enormous. One forward pass over a sequence of length n yields n separate next-token predictions — every position simultaneously serves as a training example, each with the correct restricted view of its prefix. This is teacher forcing: the model conditions on the true prefix rather than its own generations. A sequence of 8192 tokens therefore produces 8192 supervised examples for the cost of a single parallel pass, which is exactly the property the RNN could not offer.

Encoder-decoder vs decoder-only, and why decoder-only won

The 2017 paper described an encoder-decoder model for translation: a bidirectional encoder reads the source, and a decoder attends to both its own prefix (causally) and the encoder output (via cross-attention). Three families descend from that original design.

FamilyAttentionObjectiveExamplesBest at
Encoder-onlyBidirectionalMasked token predictionBERT (Devlin et al., 2018)Classification, embeddings, retrieval
Encoder-decoderBidirectional + causal + crossSpan corruption / seq2seqT5 (Raffel et al., 2019), BARTFixed input-to-output transduction
Decoder-onlyCausal throughoutNext-token predictionGPT-2/3, Llama, MistralOpen-ended generation, general-purpose LLMs

The decisive advantage of decoder-only is training-signal density. BERT-style masked language modeling corrupts and predicts roughly 15% of tokens, so most of each forward pass produces no direct loss term. T5-style span corruption is similar. Causal language modeling extracts a prediction from every single position. Per unit of compute spent, the decoder-only model gets several times the supervised signal, and when the binding constraint is compute (see section 2), that ratio dominates.

The second advantage is that a single format subsumes every task. An encoder-decoder model presumes a clean split between an input to be read and an output to be produced. A decoder-only model just continues a token stream, so translation, summarization, dialogue, few-shot classification and code completion are all the same operation on differently-formatted prefixes. This is what makes in-context learning natural — demonstrations are simply part of the prefix — and it is the property GPT-3 (Brown et al., 2020) demonstrated at scale in Language Models are Few-Shot Learners.

The third advantage is inference-time: KV caching. Because the causal mask guarantees earlier positions never attend to later ones, the key and value vectors computed for a token remain valid for every subsequent generation step and can simply be cached. Generating token t+1 costs one position of work, not t+1. A bidirectional encoder cannot do this, since appending a token changes every position's representation. Section 6 covers the cost that this cache imposes on memory.

The honest caveat is that decoder-only is not provably superior in representational terms. Bidirectional encoders remain the better choice for embeddings and retrieval, where you want a whole-sequence representation and generation is not required; encoder-decoder models remain competitive on well-specified transduction tasks. Decoder-only won the general-purpose LLM race for reasons of training efficiency, uniformity and inference economics, not because attention over a prefix is inherently more expressive.

Gotcha The most common misconception is that attention is where a transformer's knowledge lives — the architecture is named after it, so it absorbs all the attention, so to speak. In parameter terms the opposite is true: at the classic 4× expansion the FFN sublayers hold roughly twice the parameters of the attention sublayers, and interpretability work locates much of a model's factual recall in those FFN layers rather than in attention. Attention is the routing mechanism that moves information between positions; the FFN is the storage and computation. Two practical consequences follow. First, MoE (section 4) sparsifies the FFN specifically, because that is where the parameters worth sparsifying are. Second, the quadratic cost of attention in sequence length does not mean attention dominates the FLOP count — at typical training sequence lengths the FFN is still the larger share of compute, and attention only overtakes it at long context. Conflating “quadratic in n” with “the majority of the compute” leads to badly mis-targeted optimization.

title: Pretraining & Scaling Laws
summary: Next-token prediction as pretraining, compute-optimal scaling (Chinchilla), emergent capabilities, loss curves.
html:
Pretraining is where nearly all of a language model's capability originates, and it consumes nearly all of the compute budget. Everything in post-training — instruction tuning, RLHF, reasoning training — adjusts and elicits capability that pretraining already created. This section covers the objective itself, the empirical laws that govern how it scales, and the practical decisions those laws drive.

Next-token prediction as the objective

The entire pretraining objective is: given a prefix, predict the next token. Formally, maximize the log-likelihood the model assigns to the actual continuation, which is minimizing cross-entropy loss:

L = -(1/N) * sum over t of log P(x_t | x_1, ..., x_{t-1}; theta)

Cross-entropy has a concrete interpretation worth holding onto: it is the average number of nats needed to encode the true next token under the model's distribution. Divide by ln(2) to get bits per token. A loss of 2.0 nats means the model is about as uncertain as a uniform choice among e<sup>2</sup> ≈ 7.4 equally likely tokens. Perplexity is just exp(L), the same quantity in "effective vocabulary size" units. This is why language modeling is fundamentally a compression problem: a better model is a better compressor of text, and the loss is the compression rate.

Teacher forcing is the training convention where the model always conditions on the ground-truth prefix rather than its own previous predictions. Combined with causal masking (section 1.8), this is what makes training parallel: every position is evaluated simultaneously against the true prefix, so one forward pass over n tokens produces n loss terms. The known cost is exposure bias — at generation time the model conditions on its own output, a distribution it never trained on, so errors can compound. In practice this matters far less than early theory predicted, and every frontier model is trained this way.

Why such a trivial objective produces general capability is the genuinely interesting question. The argument that has held up is that next-token prediction on a sufficiently diverse corpus is not a narrow task but an implicit multi-task objective. To predict the token after “the capital of Australia is” requires a fact. After a proof's penultimate line, a deduction. After 200 lines of a Python function, a model of program state. After a character's dialogue in a novel, a model of that character's beliefs. Because the corpus contains text whose continuation depends on essentially any competence humans express in writing, driving the loss down forces the model to acquire those competences instrumentally. Compression and understanding converge: the shortest description of a corpus of physics papers is one that has internalized physics.

The caveat is that this argument justifies capability, not truthfulness or alignment. The objective is to model the distribution of text, and text contains falsehoods, inconsistencies and bad reasoning in proportion to their frequency in the corpus. A perfectly-optimized language model reproduces the corpus distribution faithfully, including its errors. That gap is the entire justification for post-training, and it is why base models are not usable products.

The compute budget equation

Scaling arguments require a way to count compute. The standard approximation for a dense transformer is:

C  ~=  6 * N * D

C = total training compute in FLOPs
N = number of (non-embedding) parameters
D = number of training tokens

Where the 6 comes from. Take a single parameter in a weight matrix and a single token. In the forward pass, that parameter participates in one multiply and one add — 2 FLOPs. The backward pass computes two sets of gradients: with respect to the layer's inputs (to keep propagating backwards) and with respect to the weights themselves. Each costs about as much as the forward pass, so backward is roughly 2× forward, or 4 FLOPs. Total: 2 forward + 4 backward = 6 FLOPs per parameter per token. Multiply by N parameters and D tokens and you have C = 6ND. The corresponding inference figure is 2N per token, since inference is forward-only — a useful number for section 2.7.

What the approximation ignores. It counts only matrix-multiply FLOPs in the weights, omitting attention's Q @ K.T and weights @ V operations, which do not involve parameters and scale with sequence length rather than parameter count. That term is genuinely negligible at short context and genuinely is not at long context — for a model with d_model of a few thousand, attention's share becomes significant once sequence length reaches the tens of thousands. It also ignores embedding parameters (hence "non-embedding N") and activation recomputation, which trades extra forward FLOPs for memory and can push the effective constant above 6. Treat 6ND as a good first-order estimate that needs correction in the long-context regime.

Kaplan et al. (2020): the original scaling laws

Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models (Kaplan et al., 2020) established the empirical result that reframed the field: test loss falls as a power law in model size, dataset size and compute, smoothly and predictably over many orders of magnitude.

L(N) ~= (N_c / N) ** alpha_N        # loss vs parameters
L(D) ~= (D_c / D) ** alpha_D        # loss vs data
L(C) ~= (C_c / C) ** alpha_C        # loss vs compute

A power law is a straight line on a log-log plot, and that is the practical content of the finding. Fit the line on small, cheap models and you can extrapolate the loss of a model far larger than any you have trained. This converted large-model training from a gamble into a forecastable engineering exercise: you can justify a nine-figure training run because a curve fit on much cheaper runs tells you what loss you will land on. That predictive capability, more than any single number in the paper, is what made frontier-scale investment rational.

Two further findings mattered. First, the exponents are small — loss falls slowly, so each increment of capability costs exponentially more compute. Second, and this is the part that was later corrected, Kaplan et al. concluded that when scaling a fixed compute budget, most of it should go to parameters rather than data: bigger models trained on comparatively little data, stopped well short of convergence. That conclusion directly shaped the era of GPT-3 (175B parameters, roughly 300B tokens) and its contemporaries.

Chinchilla (Hoffmann et al., 2022): the correction

Training Compute-Optimal Large Language Models (Hoffmann et al., 2022) re-ran the analysis more carefully — notably tuning the learning-rate schedule to each run's length rather than holding one schedule fixed, a methodological detail that turns out to explain much of the discrepancy — and reached a materially different conclusion: model size and training tokens should scale in roughly equal proportion.

The headline heuristic is roughly 20 tokens per parameter for compute-optimal training. The verification was direct: the authors trained Chinchilla at 70B parameters on ~1.4T tokens, matching the compute of Gopher (280B parameters, ~300B tokens), and Chinchilla outperformed it broadly despite being a quarter the size.

ModelParamsTokensTokens/paramVerdict
GPT-3 (2020)175B~300B~1.7Severely undertrained
Gopher (2021)280B~300B~1.1Severely undertrained
Chinchilla (2022)70B~1.4T~20Compute-optimal
Llama 3 8B (2024)8B~15T~1875Deliberately overtrained
For a fixed compute budget, loss is U-shaped in model size: both an under-parameterized model trained on too much data and an over-parameterized model starved of tokens land above the compute-optimal minimum, and the minima across budgets trace the roughly 20-tokens-per-parameter line.

The implication for the field was immediate and large. Every major model of the preceding era was badly undertrained — there was substantial free performance available at no additional compute simply by reallocating the budget toward data. The whole field's parameter counts stopped rising and in many cases fell, while token counts rose by an order of magnitude. The bragging-rights metric quietly shifted from parameters to training tokens, and the binding constraint shifted from "can we build a model this big" to "can we source data this good" — which is what makes section 3 strategically important rather than merely technical.

Treat the specific numbers as an empirical fit, not a constant of nature. The ~20 ratio depends on the architecture, the data distribution, the tokenizer and the training setup, and reanalyses have produced somewhat different coefficients. The robust finding is the qualitative one — parameters and data should scale together, in the same ballpark of proportion — not the second decimal place.

Emergent capabilities and the metric-artifact critique

Pretraining loss falls smoothly. Performance on many specific downstream tasks does not appear to — it sits at chance across several orders of magnitude of scale, then rises sharply past some threshold. Whether that discontinuity is real is an actively contested question, and both positions deserve a fair statement.

Emergence is realEmergence is a metric artifact
Key workWei et al. (2022), Emergent Abilities of Large Language ModelsSchaeffer et al. (2023), Are Emergent Abilities of LLMs a Mirage?
ClaimSome abilities are absent at small scale and present at large scale, unpredictablyThe sharpness comes from the metric, not the model
MechanismQualitatively new capability crosses a usability thresholdAll-or-nothing metrics (exact match, accuracy) discretize smooth improvement
ImplicationScaling produces genuine surprises; safety-relevant capabilities may appear without warningProgress is smooth and forecastable; use continuous metrics and the sharpness disappears

The critique's argument is specific and worth understanding mechanically. Consider a task scored by exact match on a 5-digit arithmetic answer. Suppose per-digit accuracy improves smoothly with scale. Exact-match accuracy is roughly per-digit accuracy raised to the fifth power — so a smooth rise in the underlying quantity produces a sharply convex, apparently sudden rise in the reported score. Schaeffer et al. showed that swapping to a continuous metric such as token edit distance, or measuring per-digit accuracy directly, converts many published emergence curves into smooth ones. Under that reading, the model was improving continuously all along and the metric was hiding it.

What each side concedes. The emergence side largely accepts that discontinuous metrics exaggerate sharpness and that some published examples dissolve under better measurement. The artifact side largely accepts that the practical situation is unchanged: if the task you care about is scored by exact match — and many real tasks genuinely are all-or-nothing — then the capability really does become usable abruptly, whatever the underlying curve looks like. The live disagreement is narrower than the headlines suggest: it is about whether anything unpredictable happens in the model's internal capability, not about whether benchmark curves can look sharp.

Why this matters beyond taxonomy. If capabilities can appear without warning, pre-deployment safety evaluation cannot rely on extrapolating from smaller models, and dangerous-capability thresholds could be crossed unexpectedly. If everything is smooth underneath, capability forecasting from small-scale runs is sound provided you measure with continuous metrics. Frontier labs' evaluation practice largely hedges: forecast with continuous metrics where possible, but test the actual deployed scale directly rather than trusting extrapolation.

Reading loss curves in practice

The training loss curve is the primary instrument during a large run, and practitioners read specific things from it.

ObservationUsual meaningTypical response
Straight line on log-log axesHealthy power-law progressNothing — this is the goal
Sharp isolated spike, self-recoveringA bad batch or a transient numerical eventNote it; usually tolerable
Spike that does not recoverDivergence; often numerical instabilityRoll back to a checkpoint, skip the offending data, lower LR
Early plateau at high lossLR too high, or bad initializationRestart with revised warmup or LR
Train falls, held-out risesOverfittingRare in single-epoch web-scale pretraining; check for data repetition
Visible step down at a data-mix changeCurriculum or annealing phase transitionExpected if intentional

Loss spikes are a genuine operational hazard at scale, not a curiosity. Large runs spike; the reported mitigations include skipping the data batches involved, restarting from an earlier checkpoint, lowering the learning rate, and numerical-precision fixes. The reason a rollback is even possible is frequent checkpointing, which is standard practice precisely because a diverged run that cannot be rewound wastes the entire budget spent so far.

Loss values are only comparable within a fixed tokenizer. Cross-entropy is per token, so a tokenizer that packs more characters into each token yields a higher per-token loss for identical modeling quality. Comparing raw loss between models with different vocabularies is meaningless; normalize to bits per byte or per character first. This trips people up constantly when comparing published numbers across model families.

Learning rate schedules, batch size, and critical batch size

Warmup then decay is the near-universal schedule. Learning rate rises linearly from zero over some hundreds or thousands of steps, then decays — classically following a cosine to roughly 10% of peak by the end of training.

lr(t) = peak_lr * t / warmup                       # t < warmup
lr(t) = min_lr + 0.5*(peak_lr - min_lr)
        * (1 + cos(pi * (t - warmup)/(T - warmup))) # after warmup

Warmup exists because early training is where the model is most fragile. At initialization the parameters are random and the gradients are large and poorly-conditioned; a full-size step can knock the model into a region it never recovers from. Adam's second-moment estimates are also poorly estimated in the first steps, making its effective step size unreliable. Ramping up gives those statistics time to stabilize. Pre-norm architectures (section 1.5) reduce but do not eliminate the need.

The decay matters more than it looks. A large fraction of the final loss improvement arrives during the last portion of the decay, which is why loss curves show a characteristic drop near the end. This creates a real practical annoyance: because cosine decay is defined against a predetermined total step count, a run stopped early is not merely a shorter run — it is a run that never got its decay, and its loss is correspondingly worse than the curve suggests. This is exactly the methodological issue implicated in the Kaplan-versus-Chinchilla discrepancy. It is also why constant-then-decay schedules, where a constant phase is followed by a short decay that can be launched at any point, have become attractive for runs of uncertain length.

Critical batch size is the concept that governs how much data parallelism actually buys. Increasing batch size reduces gradient noise, so larger batches permit larger, better-directed steps — up to a point. Below the critical batch size, doubling the batch roughly halves the steps needed, so the extra hardware converts directly into wall-clock speedup. Above it, gradients are already near-noiseless, additional samples mostly confirm what the previous ones said, and doubling the batch buys progressively less. McCandlish et al. (2018) formalized this in An Empirical Model of Large-Batch Training, connecting it to the gradient noise scale.

The practical consequence is a tradeoff between wall-clock time and total compute. Training past the critical batch size still finishes sooner in wall-clock terms if you have the hardware — it just burns more total FLOPs to reach the same loss. Frontier labs frequently accept that trade, because calendar time is a competitive variable and idle accelerators have no salvage value. Critical batch size also grows as training proceeds and loss falls, which motivates batch-size ramps that increase the batch over the course of a run.

Overtraining past Chinchilla-optimal

Chinchilla answers the question “given a fixed training budget, what minimizes loss?” That is frequently the wrong question, and Llama-family models train far past the compute-optimal point on purpose. Llama 3 8B saw roughly 15T tokens — on the order of a hundred times the Chinchilla-optimal allocation for its size.

The reason is that for a deployed model, inference cost dominates training cost. Training is paid once. Inference is paid per token served, forever, across every user. Recall from section 2.2 that inference costs about 2N FLOPs per token, a function of parameter count alone — a model half the size is about half the cost on every request it ever serves, and also halves the memory footprint, which determines how many concurrent requests fit on a GPU and hence the achievable batch size.

So the objective changes shape. Instead of minimizing loss for a fixed training budget, you minimize total lifetime cost — training plus expected inference — subject to a target quality. That objective systematically favors a smaller model trained much longer: you accept a worse loss-per-training-FLOP in exchange for a permanently cheaper model at a given quality level. At serving volumes where inference FLOPs eventually exceed training FLOPs, the extra training pays for itself.

ObjectiveOptimal shapeWho chooses it
Minimize loss per training FLOPChinchilla-optimal, ~20 tokens/paramResearch runs, scaling-law studies
Minimize total training + inference costSmaller model, heavily overtrainedWidely deployed production models
Maximize absolute capability, cost asideLargest trainable model, well-fed with dataFrontier capability demonstrations

The limit is diminishing returns, not a hard wall. Returns to additional tokens keep falling and data quality becomes the binding constraint well before the mathematics stops working — you run out of good text before you run out of reasons to keep training (section 3.8). Distillation from a larger teacher is the other standard route to the same goal of a small, cheap, strong model.

Gotcha Scaling laws are empirical curve fits over a limited observed range, not physical laws — and the field's own history proves it. Kaplan et al. (2020) was the authoritative account for two years, drove the design of GPT-3-era models, and was then substantially revised by Chinchilla, which showed those models were badly undertrained. The correction came significantly from a methodological detail in learning-rate scheduling, not from new physics. Anyone quoting “20 tokens per parameter” as a constant is repeating a fit whose coefficients depend on architecture, tokenizer, data distribution and optimizer, and which has already been revised once. Two specific failure modes follow: extrapolating a fit far past the compute range where it was measured, and assuming the exponents transfer across a change of architecture (dense to MoE, say) or data mix. The reliable content of this literature is the shape — smooth power-law improvement, parameters and data scaling together — not any particular constant.

title: Tokenization & Data
summary: BPE and its variants, vocabulary size tradeoffs, data curation/dedup/filtering, the data wall.
html:
Tokenization and data curation are the two least glamorous parts of building a language model and two of the highest-leverage. The tokenizer determines the units the model reasons in and is frozen for the model's entire life; the data determines what the model knows and, after Chinchilla, is the binding constraint on frontier training. A large share of production model failures trace back to one of these two rather than to the architecture.

Why tokenization exists

A transformer needs a finite vocabulary of discrete symbols. Text is not natively discrete at any convenient granularity, so a choice must be made, and the two obvious options are both bad.

GranularityVocab sizeSequence lengthFatal problem
Character / byte~100 / 256Very longAttention is quadratic in length; long-range dependencies span thousands of positions
WordUnbounded in principleShortOut-of-vocabulary words; huge embedding matrix; morphology unlearnable
Subword (BPE etc.)~30k–250kModerateThe compromise everyone uses — see 3.5 for its pathologies

The character-level problem is compute. English averages roughly 4–5 characters per word, so character tokenization inflates sequence length several-fold. Since attention costs scale quadratically in sequence length, a 5× longer sequence is roughly 25× the attention cost, and every semantic dependency is stretched across five times as many positions. Character-level models are not impossible — they work — but they spend most of their capacity relearning that letters compose into words.

The word-level problem is the open vocabulary. Natural language has no finite word list: names, typos, compounds, URLs, code identifiers and new coinages arrive continuously. Any fixed word vocabulary maps everything it has not seen to a single <UNK> token, destroying information irrecoverably. Worse, the embedding and output projection matrices scale with vocabulary size, so a million-word vocabulary at d_model = 4096 costs about 4B parameters in each of two matrices, spent largely on words seen a handful of times. Morphologically rich languages make this dramatically worse, since a single Finnish or Turkish stem generates hundreds of surface forms that a word vocabulary treats as unrelated atoms.

Subword tokenization resolves both by letting frequency decide granularity. Common words get a single token; rare words decompose into pieces; anything unseen still decomposes into something. The vocabulary stays fixed and modest while remaining able to represent arbitrary text.

Byte-Pair Encoding, mechanically

BPE was a compression algorithm (Gage, 1994) repurposed for NLP by Sennrich et al. (2015) in Neural Machine Translation of Rare Words with Subword Units. Training the tokenizer is a greedy, iterative merge procedure over a corpus.

1. Start with the vocabulary = all individual characters (or all 256 bytes).
2. Split the corpus into these atomic symbols.
3. Count every adjacent symbol pair across the corpus.
4. Take the MOST FREQUENT pair, merge it into one new symbol,
   add it to the vocabulary, and record the merge rule.
5. Repeat from 3 until the vocabulary reaches the target size.

A worked miniature. Suppose the corpus is low low lower newest newest. Initially every character is a symbol. The pair (l, o) is frequent, so it merges to lo. Then (lo, w) merges to low. Separately (e, s) merges to es, then (es, t) to est, and eventually newest may become a single symbol while lower remains low + er. Note what this produces without being told to: est and er are recognizable English morphemes, discovered purely from co-occurrence statistics. That is BPE's appeal — frequency-driven merging approximates morphology for free, with no linguistic knowledge encoded.

BPE starts from single characters and repeatedly merges the most frequent adjacent pair into a new symbol, so subword units like low, er and est emerge from corpus statistics alone; encoding new text replays those merge rules in the order they were learned.

The learned artifact is an ordered list of merge rules, and the order is load-bearing. Encoding new text replays those merges in exactly the order they were learned: split into atomic symbols, then apply merge rules by rank until none apply. Because the ranking is fixed, encoding is deterministic and any string is representable. Decoding is a simple lookup and concatenation.

Two consequences follow directly from the greedy construction. First, the tokenizer is corpus-specific — a BPE vocabulary trained on English web text will segment code or Japanese poorly, because the merges that would have helped were never frequent enough to be learned. Second, the tokenizer is trained before the model and frozen for its lifetime; changing it invalidates every learned embedding and effectively requires retraining. Tokenizer decisions are therefore among the most expensive-to-reverse choices in the whole pipeline.

Variants: WordPiece, SentencePiece, byte-level BPE

SchemeMerge criterionHandles raw bytes?Used by
BPEHighest pair frequencyNot inherentlyOriginal GPT, many others
WordPieceHighest likelihood gain, not raw countNo — uses [UNK]BERT
Unigram LMPrune from a large seed vocab by likelihood lossVia SentencePieceT5, ALBERT
Byte-level BPEPair frequency, over bytesYes — no OOV possibleGPT-2/3/4, Llama, most modern LLMs

WordPiece changes the selection criterion. Rather than merging the most frequent pair, it merges the pair that most increases the likelihood of the training corpus under a unigram language model — roughly, it prefers a pair whose joint frequency exceeds what its parts' independent frequencies would predict. This favors merges that are genuinely informative units over merges that are merely common.

The Unigram LM approach inverts the direction entirely. Instead of growing a vocabulary by merging, it starts from a large candidate vocabulary and iteratively prunes the pieces whose removal costs the least corpus likelihood. A useful side effect is that it defines a probability over multiple valid segmentations of the same string, enabling subword regularization — sampling different segmentations during training as a form of data augmentation, which BPE's deterministic greedy encoding cannot naturally do.

SentencePiece is best understood as an implementation framework rather than an algorithm. It implements both BPE and Unigram, and its distinctive contribution is treating input as a raw stream including spaces — whitespace is encoded as a visible meta-symbol rather than stripped by a pre-tokenizer. This makes tokenization fully reversible (decode reconstructs the input exactly, spaces included) and language-agnostic, which matters greatly for languages such as Chinese, Japanese and Thai that do not delimit words with spaces at all. Pipelines that pre-split on whitespace are implicitly assuming a European writing system.

Byte-level BPE is the modern default, and its key property is that out-of-vocabulary is structurally impossible. Introduced with GPT-2 (Radford et al., 2019), it runs BPE over UTF-8 bytes rather than Unicode characters. Since the base vocabulary is all 256 byte values, and every possible string is a byte sequence, every input is representable — no <UNK> token is needed for any text in any language, plus emoji, binary-ish content and malformed encodings. The cost is that non-ASCII text pays a multi-byte penalty: a character encoded in three UTF-8 bytes needs merges to be learned before it becomes a single token, and if it was rare in the tokenizer's training corpus, those merges do not exist. This is a direct cause of the fairness issue in section 3.5.

Vocabulary size tradeoffs

Vocabulary size is a genuine optimization with costs on both sides, and modern models have drifted upward — from GPT-2's ~50k to ~128k in Llama 3 and ~256k in some multilingual models.

Effect of a LARGER vocabularyDirection
Tokens needed per documentDown (better compression)
Transformer compute per documentDown (fewer positions to process)
Effective context in charactersUp (more text fits in the same token budget)
Embedding + output matrix parametersUp (linear in vocab size)
Softmax cost over the vocabularyUp
Training examples per token embeddingDown (rare tokens are seen less)

The compute tradeoff has a clean shape. The embedding and unembedding matrices each cost vocab_size × d_model parameters, so at d_model = 4096 a 128k vocabulary spends about 0.5B parameters per matrix. That is charged once. Against it, better compression reduces the sequence length of every document processed for the entire life of the model, and transformer cost scales with sequence length. For large models trained on many tokens, the amortized win from compression generally outweighs the fixed embedding cost, which is why vocabularies have grown as models have.

The limit is the rare-token problem. Push the vocabulary large enough and the tail consists of tokens appearing a handful of times in the entire corpus. Their embeddings receive almost no gradient signal and remain close to their initialization — effectively random vectors sitting in the model's input space. These undertrained embeddings are the direct cause of the glitch tokens in the next section.

Tokenization pathologies

Tokenization is the source of a surprising share of the strange behavior people attribute to reasoning failures.

Arithmetic and number tokenization. If the tokenizer segments numbers by frequency, 1234 might become 123 + 4 while 1235 becomes 1 + 235 — inconsistent groupings that share no positional structure. Digit-place alignment, which every arithmetic algorithm depends on, is destroyed before the model sees the input. This is a major contributor to poor multi-digit arithmetic, and the fix is a tokenizer change rather than a model change: several modern tokenizers force digits to split individually or into consistent fixed-size groups, which measurably improves arithmetic.

Leading-space handling. In most byte-level BPE tokenizers the space attaches to the following word, so " the" and "the" are different tokens with different embeddings. A prompt ending in a trailing space therefore puts the model in an unusual state — it must now predict a continuation that does not begin with a space, which is rare in training. The practical rule is to never end a prompt with a trailing space; the symptom is inexplicably degraded output.

Glitch tokens. The well-known example is SolidGoldMagikarp, one of a cluster of strings identified by community researchers in 2023 that caused GPT-2 and GPT-3-era models to behave erratically — evading, hallucinating, or emitting unrelated text when asked to repeat them. The mechanism is a mismatch between the tokenizer's training corpus and the model's: these strings (Reddit usernames, subreddit names, artifacts of scraped logs) were frequent enough in the tokenizer's corpus to earn dedicated tokens, but were filtered out or vanishingly rare in the model's training data. The result is a token with a nearly untrained embedding — a random vector in input space that the model has no learned response to. The lesson generalizes: train the tokenizer and the model on distributions that match.

Non-English compression disparity, which is both a fairness and a cost problem. Tokenizers trained on predominantly English corpora compress English efficiently and other languages poorly. The same semantic content can take several times more tokens in a language with limited representation in the tokenizer's corpus, and the penalty falls hardest on languages with non-Latin scripts, where byte-level fallback charges multiple bytes per character. Three concrete harms follow: API pricing is per token, so identical work costs more in those languages; the effective context window is proportionally smaller; and latency is worse. Petrov et al. (2023) documented these disparities across tokenizers, and multilingual-first tokenizers with larger vocabularies are the main mitigation.

Character-level tasks are hard for reasons that have nothing to do with reasoning. Asking a model to count letters in a word or reverse a string is asking it to introspect on structure inside a token it perceives as an atom. The model sees an opaque symbol, not a spelled-out sequence. This is why such tasks fail in ways that seem inconsistent with the model's other abilities — it is an input representation limit, not a competence limit.

Web-scale corpus construction

After Chinchilla, data volume became a first-class constraint, and a public lineage of increasingly well-filtered corpora emerged.

CorpusOriginContribution
Common CrawlOngoing public web crawlThe raw substrate under nearly every large corpus; petabytes, mostly junk
C4Raffel et al., 2019 (with T5)Cleaned Common Crawl; showed heuristic filtering materially helps
The PileGao et al., 2020 (EleutherAI)825GB curated mix of 22 sources; established diverse-domain mixing
RefinedWebPenedo et al., 2023 (with Falcon)Argued rigorously filtered web data alone can match curated corpora
FineWebHuggingFace, 2024Large open web corpus with ablation-driven filtering; FineWeb-Edu subset

Common Crawl is the substrate and it is mostly unusable as-is — boilerplate, navigation chrome, SEO spam, machine-translated filler, adult content and near-duplicate templated pages. The entire art is in what you remove. C4 demonstrated the point with simple heuristics (drop lines without terminal punctuation, drop pages with too few sentences, deduplicate, filter a blocklist) and showed that models trained on the cleaned version beat models trained on more raw data.

The Pile made the case for deliberate domain mixing, combining web text with books, arXiv, PubMed, GitHub, Stack Exchange, patents and subtitles. Its influence was as much sociological as technical: it was openly available and documented, which made rigorous comparison possible for people outside large labs.

RefinedWeb challenged an assumption the field had accepted. The prevailing belief was that curated high-quality sources such as books and Wikipedia were essential and that web text was filler. Penedo et al. (2023) showed that web data filtered and deduplicated aggressively enough could match or exceed curated-corpus models. This mattered strategically, because web data is far more abundant than curated data — if filtering quality substitutes for source curation, the ceiling is much higher.

FineWeb continued the trend with published ablations rather than asserted heuristics, and its FineWeb-Edu subset — filtered by a classifier scoring educational value — reinforced a consistent finding: aggressive filtering toward a narrower, higher-quality distribution often beats retaining more tokens.

Deduplication, filtering, and mixing

Deduplication is one of the highest-return operations available, and the empirical case is strong. Lee et al. (2021), in Deduplicating Training Data Makes Language Models Better, found that web corpora contain very substantial duplication, and that removing it improves models while requiring fewer training steps, reduces memorization and verbatim regurgitation of training data, and eliminates train/test contamination where benchmark items appear in the training set.

Exact deduplication is easy; near-duplicate detection is the real work. Exact matching by hash catches identical documents but misses the dominant case — the same article across mirrors with different headers, ads and boilerplate. The standard tool is MinHash combined with locality-sensitive hashing:

1. Represent each document as its set of n-grams (shingles).
2. MinHash: apply k hash functions; keep the minimum value under each.
   Probability two docs share a min-hash = their Jaccard similarity.
3. LSH: band the signatures and hash each band; documents colliding
   in ANY band become candidate pairs.
4. Verify candidates exactly; cluster and keep one representative.

The reason this matters at scale is that comparing every pair of documents is quadratic and utterly infeasible at web scale; LSH converts the problem into approximately linear-time bucketing, at the cost of a tunable false-negative rate.

Quality filtering comes in three families, usually stacked. Heuristic filters are cheap rules — document length bounds, punctuation ratios, symbol-to-word ratios, repeated-line detection, blocklists. Classifier-based filtering trains a lightweight model to score documents against a reference set of known-good text; GPT-3's pipeline used a classifier of this kind, and FineWeb-Edu's educational-quality classifier is a refined descendant. Perplexity-based filtering scores documents under a small reference language model and drops the extremes — very high perplexity indicates gibberish, while very low perplexity often indicates boilerplate or repetition.

The recurring trap in classifier-based filtering is distributional narrowing. A classifier trained to prefer Wikipedia-like text will systematically down-weight dialects, informal registers, and topics underrepresented in the reference set. You are not filtering for quality in the abstract; you are filtering toward whatever your reference corpus looks like, with all its demographic and topical skew. Filtering aggressively along one axis quietly narrows the distribution along others.

Data mixing weights are a real and largely undisclosed lever. Given code, web text, books, math, papers and multilingual text, the proportions materially change the resulting model — and notably, including a substantial share of code appears to improve general reasoning benchmarks, not just coding ability, a widely-reported finding whose mechanism is not settled. Methods like DoReMi (Xie et al., 2023) optimize domain weights algorithmically rather than by hand. Frontier labs treat their mixtures as core intellectual property, so published detail is thin, and the optimal mixture remains genuinely unresolved rather than merely secret.

Curriculum and annealing. Rather than one fixed mixture throughout, it is now common to shift the distribution over training — typically finishing with a phase weighted toward the highest-quality data at a decayed learning rate. Given how much of the final loss improvement arrives during LR decay (section 2.7), what the model sees in that window has outsized influence.

Synthetic data, model collapse, and the data wall

The data wall is the argument that high-quality human text is a finite resource being approached. Villalobos et al. (2022, updated since) estimated the stock of public human-generated text and projected that frontier training runs would exhaust the high-quality portion within a small number of years at prevailing growth rates. Whether it constitutes a hard wall is contested — the estimates involve real uncertainty about what counts as usable, and multi-epoch training, non-public data, non-text modalities and better filtering all extend the runway — but the direction is not seriously disputed: data has replaced compute as the tighter constraint at the frontier.

Synthetic data is the leading proposed answer, and it demonstrably works in specific regimes. The regimes where it works share a common feature: verifiability. Generated code can be executed against tests; mathematical derivations can be checked; formal proofs can be verified by a proof assistant. In those cases the generator can be run at volume and its output filtered by ground truth, so the resulting data carries genuine signal rather than only the generator's existing beliefs. The Phi model family (Microsoft, from 2023) pursued textbook-quality synthetic data explicitly, and distillation from a stronger teacher is the same idea in another guise.

Model collapse is the failure mode when that verification is absent. Shumailov et al. (2023) showed that recursively training models on the output of previous models degrades them across generations. The mechanism is statistical rather than mysterious: sampling from a model under-represents the tails of the true distribution, so each generation trains on a slightly narrowed distribution, and narrowing compounds. Rare events disappear first, variance shrinks, and the model converges toward its own most-probable outputs. The important qualifier — and it is the one most often dropped when this result is cited — is that collapse is demonstrated under recursive replacement, where synthetic data supplants real data. Accumulating synthetic data alongside a persistent base of real data behaves far better, and verified or filtered synthetic data is a different situation again.

Synthetic data settingOutlook
Verifiable output (code with tests, checkable math, formal proofs)Works well; verification provides genuine signal
Distillation from a stronger teacherWorks; transfers real capability downward
Augmentation mixed with a persistent real-data baseGenerally fine; collapse results do not directly apply
Recursive self-training replacing real dataDocumented degradation; the collapse regime
Unverifiable factual contentRisky — cannot generate knowledge the generator lacks

The principled limit is that synthetic data cannot manufacture information that was never there. It can restructure, filter, amplify and make explicit what a model already encodes, and combined with verification it can extract genuinely new correct examples. It cannot conjure facts about the world absent from the original training distribution. As of the early-2025 literature, whether synthetic data fully substitutes for scarce human text at the frontier is an open question, and the honest answer is that it clearly helps in verifiable domains and remains unproven in general ones.

Gotcha When a model fails at counting the letters in a word, comparing 9.11 against 9.9, or doing multi-digit arithmetic, the instinct is to call it a reasoning failure. Frequently it is a tokenization failure, and the distinction matters because it changes the fix entirely. The model does not see characters — it sees opaque subword symbols, and asking it to introspect on the letters inside one is asking about structure its input representation discarded. Number tokenization is the sharpest case: inconsistent digit grouping destroys the place-value alignment that every arithmetic procedure requires, before the model computes anything at all. The diagnostic habit worth building is to check how a failing input actually tokenizes before concluding anything about the model's reasoning. The corollary for the safety and evaluation side is that a benchmark can be measuring tokenizer artifacts while appearing to measure reasoning — and results will then fail to transfer across model families with different tokenizers, for reasons that have nothing to do with capability.

title: Mixture of Experts & Sparsity
summary: Sparse MoE layers, routing/load balancing, why sparsity buys capacity without proportional compute.
html:
Mixture of Experts breaks the assumption that every token must be processed by every parameter. In a dense transformer, parameter count and per-token compute are locked together — doubling one doubles the other. MoE decouples them, letting a model hold vastly more knowledge than it spends compute on for any single token. The technique is widely believed to be in use across frontier models, and it converts a compute problem into a communication and memory problem, which is a trade worth understanding precisely.

The motivation: decoupling capacity from compute

Recall from section 2.2 that a dense transformer costs about 2N FLOPs per token at inference and 6N per token in training, where N is the parameter count. This proportionality is the constraint MoE attacks.

The observation motivating sparsity is that most parameters are irrelevant to most tokens. A dense model applies its full parameter set to every token regardless of content — the weights encoding Portuguese morphology are multiplied against a token in a Python file, contributing nothing but consuming exactly as much compute as the weights that matter. Since a model's knowledge is broad but any single token engages a narrow slice of it, forcing every token through every parameter is wasteful in a specific, exploitable way.

The MoE proposition: maintain many parameter subsets ("experts"), and for each token activate only a few. A model with 8 experts per layer that activates 2 holds roughly 4× the FFN parameters of a comparable dense model while performing roughly the same FLOPs per token. Capacity scales with total experts; compute scales with experts activated. The two are now independent knobs.

The empirical payoff is better loss per unit of training compute. Sparse models reliably reach a given loss with less compute than dense models, or a better loss at matched compute. What they do not do is come free — the costs simply move from FLOPs to memory and communication, which sections 4.5 through 4.7 cover.

The sparse MoE layer

MoE replaces the FFN sublayer, not attention — a choice that follows directly from section 1.6. The FFN holds roughly twice the parameters of attention per layer, and it operates independently per position with no cross-token interaction, which makes it trivially separable into parallel experts. Attention's entire job is mixing information between tokens, so it resists this decomposition. Attention stays dense and shared; the FFN becomes N independent expert FFNs plus a router.

# Dense block
h = x + Attention(RMSNorm(x))
y = h + FFN(RMSNorm(h))

# MoE block  (attention unchanged)
h = x + Attention(RMSNorm(h_in))
z = RMSNorm(h)
gate_logits = z @ W_router              # (n_experts,)
top_vals, top_idx = topk(gate_logits, k)
weights = softmax(top_vals)             # softmax over the k selected
y = h + sum over j in top_idx of
        weights[j] * Expert_j(z)

Routing is per token, not per sequence — a detail that is easy to skim past and matters enormously. Every token at every MoE layer is routed independently, so a single sequence of 2000 tokens produces 2000 independent routing decisions per layer. Successive tokens routinely go to different experts, and a token's expert assignment changes from layer to layer.

Typical configurations use k = 1 or k = 2. Switch Transformer (Fedus et al., 2021) showed k = 1 works, which was surprising at the time — the prior assumption was that at least two experts were needed for the gating to receive useful gradient signal. Mixtral 8x7B uses 8 experts with k = 2. Some more recent designs use many more, finer-grained experts with a higher k, plus a shared expert that every token passes through to capture common computation.

The routing mechanism

Top-2 routing: the router scores all experts, the two highest run, and their outputs are combined weighted by the router's softmax over the selected scores.

The router is remarkably simple — usually a single learned matrix mapping the token's hidden state to one logit per expert. No hidden layers, no separate training procedure. Its cost is negligible against the experts it dispatches to.

How the router learns, and the discreteness problem it works around. The router is trained by ordinary backpropagation of the main loss, with no separate supervision — there is no label saying which expert should handle a token. The gradient path works because the selected experts' outputs are multiplied by their softmax gate weights. If expert j's output reduces the loss, the gradient increases weight[j], which increases gate_logits[j], which makes the router more likely to select expert j for similar tokens. Expert specialization is therefore emergent, not designed. The subtlety is that topk is discrete and non-differentiable: gradient flows only through the weights of experts that were actually selected, never through the unselected ones. The router can learn to reweight among its current choices, but it gets no direct signal about experts it did not try — a rich-get-richer dynamic that motivates section 4.4.

Learned specialization is real but often not semantically legible. Analyses of open MoE models — Mixtral's authors reported this explicitly — generally find that experts do not partition by human-recognizable topic like "code" or "biology". Specialization correlates more with syntactic and token-level regularities than with subject matter. Expect statistical structure, not an interpretable division of labor.

Load balancing and expert collapse

The central pathology of MoE training is a positive feedback loop. An expert that is selected slightly more often early in training receives more gradient updates, becomes better, and is therefore selected still more often. Left alone this converges to expert collapse: a handful of experts receive nearly all tokens while the rest remain untrained. The model then has the memory footprint of a large sparse model and the capacity of a small dense one — the worst of both.

The standard fix is an auxiliary load-balancing loss added to the training objective. The formulation from Switch Transformer multiplies, per layer, the fraction of tokens dispatched to each expert by the mean router probability assigned to it, and sums over experts:

f_i = fraction of tokens in the batch routed to expert i
P_i = mean router probability assigned to expert i over the batch

L_aux = alpha * n_experts * sum over i of (f_i * P_i)

L_total = L_task + L_aux        # alpha typically ~0.01

Why this particular product works. The sum sum(f_i * P_i) is minimized when the load is spread uniformly and maximized when it concentrates, so descending it pushes toward balance. The reason it multiplies the two quantities is the differentiability problem from section 4.3: f_i is a count and therefore has no gradient, while P_i is a smooth softmax output and does. Pairing them yields a term that is gradient-connected to the router through P_i while being scaled by the actual observed imbalance in f_i. The coefficient alpha is a genuine tuning tension: too small and experts collapse, too large and the balancing loss overrides the task loss, forcing routing decisions that ignore what the token actually needs.

Expert capacity and token dropping are the systems-side counterpart. For efficient batched execution on fixed-shape hardware buffers, each expert is allocated a fixed capacity:

capacity = capacity_factor * (tokens_per_batch / n_experts)
# capacity_factor typically 1.0 - 2.0

Tokens routed to an expert already at capacity are dropped — they skip the expert entirely and pass through on the residual connection alone. This is a real and slightly alarming property: which tokens get full computation depends on batch composition and even on their position within the batch. A higher capacity factor drops fewer tokens but wastes memory and compute on padding; a lower one is efficient but drops more. Some later formulations avoid dropping through different routing schemes — for instance letting each expert select its top tokens rather than each token selecting experts, which balances load by construction.

Training and inference behave differently here, and conflating them causes confusion. Token dropping is primarily a training-time batching artifact. At inference, serving frameworks generally aim to avoid dropping, since silently skipping computation for a user's token is not acceptable behavior.

The systems reality: communication replaces compute

MoE trades a compute bottleneck for a communication bottleneck, and this is the dominant practical difficulty. A model with 64 experts per layer cannot fit them all on one device, so experts are distributed across devices — expert parallelism. But routing is per token and content-dependent, so the tokens on any given device are routed to experts scattered across all the others.

Every MoE layer therefore requires two all-to-all collective communications: one to dispatch each token's hidden state to whichever device holds its chosen expert, and one to return the results. Every device exchanges data with every other device, twice per MoE layer, on every forward pass — and again in the backward pass.

PropertyDense modelMoE model
Dominant costMatrix multiply FLOPsAll-to-all communication
Scales badly withParameter countInterconnect bandwidth and latency
Communication patternPredictable, staticContent-dependent, varies per batch
Benefits most fromFaster arithmetic unitsFaster interconnect (NVLink, InfiniBand)

The consequence is that MoE efficiency is a property of the cluster, not the model. The same architecture that is a clear win on nodes with high-bandwidth interconnect can be a net loss across slower links, because the all-to-all stalls exceed the FLOPs saved. This is why MoE hardware-efficiency claims must always be read against the specific topology they were measured on, and why the theoretical FLOP savings routinely fail to materialize as proportional wall-clock savings. The standard mitigations are overlapping communication with computation, topology-aware expert placement, and hierarchical routing that prefers experts on the local node.

Training instabilities specific to MoE

MoE models are meaningfully harder to train stably than dense models, with failure modes that dense training simply does not have.

Router logit growth. Router logits tend to grow in magnitude during training, sharpening the softmax toward one-hot. This both amplifies the rich-get-richer collapse dynamic and creates numerical trouble in reduced precision. The standard mitigation is router z-loss, introduced in ST-MoE (Zoph et al., 2022), which penalizes the log-sum-exp of the router logits and thereby keeps them bounded.

Precision sensitivity in the router specifically. The router's decisions are discrete, so a small numerical perturbation can flip a token's expert assignment and change the computation path entirely. Standard practice is to compute the router in float32 even when the rest of the model runs in bf16 — the router is negligibly cheap, so the extra precision costs nothing and removes a whole class of nondeterminism.

Non-reproducibility from batch composition. Because expert capacity is defined per batch, a token's treatment depends on the other tokens batched with it. Change the batch composition and a token that fit before may now be dropped. This makes MoE runs harder to reproduce exactly and makes debugging harder, since a failure may not reproduce under a different batching.

Fine-tuning is disproportionately prone to overfitting. ST-MoE reported this explicitly: with a large parameter count and a comparatively small fine-tuning set, sparse models overfit more readily than dense equivalents. Mitigations include tuning only non-expert parameters, or using stronger regularization on expert weights.

Dense versus MoE: the honest tradeoff

DimensionDenseMoE
Loss per training FLOPBaselineBetter — the core advantage
Memory footprintProportional to computeMuch larger — all experts must be resident
Inference latency, batch size 1PredictableSimilar FLOPs but memory-bound and routing-dependent
Serving complexityStandardHigh — expert placement, all-to-all, load skew
Training stabilityWell understoodAdditional failure modes (4.6)
Fine-tuningStraightforwardMore overfitting-prone
Parameter count as a quality signalRoughly meaningfulMisleading — see the gotcha

The memory cost is the constraint that bites hardest in deployment. Sparsity saves compute, not memory: every expert's weights must be held in accelerator memory whether or not a given token uses them. A 47B-parameter sparse model needs 47B parameters' worth of memory even though it computes with about 13B per token. Since LLM inference is typically memory-bandwidth-bound rather than compute-bound, the FLOP savings translate into wall-clock savings far less directly than the arithmetic suggests.

Lineage and current practice

WorkYearContribution
Shazeer et al., Outrageously Large Neural Networks2017Sparsely-gated MoE layer with top-k routing and load-balancing losses, in an LSTM context
GShard (Lepikhin et al.)2020MoE in transformers at scale; expert parallelism, capacity factors, the sharding machinery
Switch Transformer (Fedus et al.)2021Simplified to top-1 routing; strong speedups at matched quality; careful stability treatment
ST-MoE (Zoph et al.)2022Router z-loss; systematic study of MoE stability and fine-tuning behavior
Mixtral 8x7B (Mistral AI)2023Openly documented, widely deployed sparse MoE with published routing analysis

Shazeer et al. (2017) established the modern formulation — the sparsely-gated layer, top-k routing and the load-balancing auxiliary loss are all present there, predating the transformer's dominance. GShard brought it to transformers with the distributed-systems machinery that made it practical. Switch Transformer simplified routing to a single expert and demonstrated large pretraining speedups at matched quality.

Mixtral 8x7B is the reference example because it is openly documented. It has 8 experts per MoE layer with top-2 routing, roughly 47B total parameters and roughly 13B active per token — the gap between those two numbers being the entire point of the architecture. Note that 47B is not 8 × 7B: attention and embeddings are shared across experts rather than replicated, so naive multiplication overcounts.

On frontier models, the honest position is inference rather than knowledge. Many frontier systems are widely believed to be MoE, and several labs have published MoE work, but architectures of closed models are generally undisclosed. As of the early-2025 literature, treat specific claims about any particular closed model's expert configuration as speculation.

Gotcha An MoE model's headline parameter count is not comparable to a dense model's, and treating it as such is the single most common error in reading model announcements. Two entirely different numbers get reported as "parameters": total parameters, which determines the memory required to hold the model, and active parameters per token, which determines the compute spent and correlates far better with capability. A 47B-total / 13B-active model performs roughly like a strong 13B-class dense model on per-token computation while demanding memory closer to a 47B dense model — so a headline "47B" invites the wrong expectation in both directions at once, overstating capability and understating hardware requirements. Always ask for both numbers.
